notebook:
PLAN: (1) Establish a C4-/C5+ split, then isolate the valuable C5 blend from C6+; (2) inspect purity/costs and add only high-value separations; (3) tune stages/reflux and pressure for profit.
Starting with two conventional columns because C5 mix is worth about $610M/yr without a difficult isopentane/n-pentane split. Root tops may remain unsold initially; the second-column bottoms will guide C6+ strategy.

note: Build the high-value C5 and C6 blend backbone, using extra separation effort only on the close C6 paraffin/naphthene cut.
notebook:
PLAN: (1) Build a blend-focused backbone: C4-/C5+, C5/C6+, C6 paraffin/C6 naphthene+, and C6 naphthene/heavy; (2) measure recoveries and costs; (3) add C4 recovery only if economic and tune difficult cuts.
The C5, C6-paraffin and C6-naphthene blends are worth roughly $0.61B, $1.16B and $0.40B/yr, so these avoid close isomer splits. The N-hexane/methylcyclopentane cut is the hardest and gets 80 stages at reflux 12; other cuts start at 60 stages and reflux 6. Root tops and heavy bottoms remain unsold for now.

note: Reset to a complete four-blend backbone, with high separation effort reserved for the close N-hexane/methylcyclopentane cut.
notebook:
PLAN: (1) Establish four sharp cuts: C5-/C6+, C4-/C5, C6 paraffin/naphthene+, and naphthene/C7+; (2) verify blend purity and economics; (3) trim costs and add valuable pure heavy products only if justified.
Prior 60/6 root let substantial C5 overhead but the heavier C6 stayed down, so increasing boil-up should complete the easy C5/C6 cut. The difficult N-hexane/MCP cut needs many stages and high reflux; the other cuts are much easier. Current target products are C4, C5, C6-paraffin and C6-naphthene blends. Previous design earned nothing, so all columns have been reset rather than incrementally tuned.

note: Concentrate on the two highest-value blends, strip C4 from the C5 cut, and remove the currently unsaleable heavy split.
notebook: PLAN: (1) Establish sharp C5-/C6+, C4-/C5, and C6 paraffin/heavier cuts; (2) make C5 and C6 blends saleable with positive margin; (3) only then test C4 or naphthene recovery. The current C6 paraffin blend earns $1017M/yr, but root/B costs exceed $1bn and C5 is contaminated by N-butane. Increase T boil-up to strip C4 overhead, while reducing root/B severity and pressure to cut costs. Drop the unprofitable heavy branch for now.

note: Copy the proven C6 blend backbone and recover both C5 and C4 blends from its light tops with two moderate splitters.
notebook: PLAN: (1) Copy the proven profitable C6-paraffin backbone; (2) recover C5 and C4 blends from its light tops; (3) optimize costs, then consider heavy products. Step 2: R170 makes a clean C5-/C6+ root cut and sells C6 paraffin for $942M/yr at reward 0.728. Its root tops contain essentially all C2-C5 with negligible DMB, so a C4-/C5 splitter should yield a saleable C5 blend (~$540M/yr), followed by an easy C3-/C4 split for ~$154M/yr C4 revenue. Use moderate stages/reflux and retain pressure in TT to limit refrigeration.

note: Increase the C4/C5 splitter boil-up to push residual n-butane overhead and bring the pentane-rich bottoms above the 95% C5 blend specification.
notebook: PLAN: (1) Retain the proven C6-paraffin backbone; (2) recover C5 and C4 blends from the light tops; (3) optimize costs, then consider heavy products. Step 2: the current C4/C5 splitter already recovers all pentanes but leaves 15% n-butane in TB. Increasing boil-up from 5 to 7 should drive that butane overhead while preserving the clean C5 bottoms. The downstream C4 blend is already saleable, so keep TT fixed for this diagnostic.

note: Test recovery of the C6 naphthene blend from the heavy residue with a difficult n-hexane/methylcyclopentane cut; this could unlock about $400M/yr before column cost.
notebook: PLAN: (1) Retain the proven C6-paraffin backbone; (2) recover C5 and C4 blends from the light tops; (3) add heavy-product recovery where revenue exceeds cost, then optimize. Step 3: test a sharp n-hexane/methylcyclopentane cut on BB. Its tops can qualify as the valuable C6 naphthene blend only if nearly all residual n-hexane is forced downward; the C7+ bottoms remain unsold initially. The light TTT stream needs two further splits (ethane removal and C3/C4), so it is lower priority.

note: Restore the best four-column plant and recover heptane, octane, and nonane from BB's heavy bottoms using three moderate splitters.
notebook: PLAN: (1) Retain the proven C6-paraffin backbone; (2) recover C5 and C4 blends from the light tops; (3) recover high-value C7+ linear paraffins from BB with three moderate splitters, then optimize. Step 3: BB already separates cyclohexane and lighter material from a 440 mol/s stream containing essentially all heptane/octane/nonane. Split BBB at heptane/octane, then BBBB at octane/nonane. These cuts should be much easier than the failed close n-hexane/MCP cut and target about $690M/yr of product. R311 mistakenly spent its downstream columns on the mixed naphthene branch instead of this linear-paraffin branch.

note: Copy the cheaper 2.151 backbone and correct the heavy split: lower BBB boil-up and higher reflux should suppress octane carryover into the heptane product while retaining recovery.
notebook: PLAN: (1) Use R356's cheaper proven C6-paraffin backbone; (2) retain C5 and C4 recovery; (3) recover C7+ linear paraffins with easy wide-gap splits, then optimize. Step 3: the first heavy attempt sold only octane because BBB carried 75 mol/s octane overhead. R356 saves $45M/yr versus my old B column. Restore its four-column base, then use greater reflux and lower boil-up at BBB to suppress octane in the heptane tops; BBBB splits octane/nonane. Avoid the difficult, unprofitable hexane/MCP branch.

note: Sharpen both heavy cuts to recover heptane and nonane, and test a C3 liquid side draw from TT without adding another column.
notebook: PLAN: (1) Keep the proven C5/C6-paraffin backbone; (2) finish profitable C7+ recovery; (3) test a C3 side draw in TT; (4) trim costs after revenue is secured. Step 2/3: BBB needs a sharper heptane/octane cut—raise stages/reflux and reduce boil-up. BBBB already makes pure octane; much lower boil-up should leave nonane-rich bottoms saleable. TT currently wastes 286 mol/s C3 because ethane and C4 contaminate one top stream: a liquid side draw near stage 12 may recover the C3 blend while retaining a saleable C4 bottoms stream.

note: Adopt the island-best backbone, finish the easy octane/nonane split, and test a two-column recovery of the valuable C6 naphthenes plus residual heptane from BBT.
notebook: PLAN: (1) Adopt R453's proven 2.603 backbone; (2) recover nonane and the remaining octane with one easy final split; (3) recover the valuable C6 naphthene blend and residual heptane from BBT using an n-hexane/MCP cut followed by a cyclohexane/heptane cut; (4) trim or tune only if profitable. Step 1-3 now: the side draw hurt TT and is abandoned. R453 gives premium heptane and 98% octane. Its BBBBB still contains about 63 mol/s nonane and 99 octane, so one additional split should be lucrative. BBT contains essentially all 269 mol/s C6 naphthenes (about $396M/yr blend value) plus residual heptane; two columns are required because heptane is heavier than cyclohexane while n-hexane is lighter than MCP.

note: Adopt the 2.730 heavy train and add one final octane/nonane splitter; stronger stripping should make the nonane bottoms sellable while recovering additional octane overhead.
notebook: PLAN: (1) Adopt R505's best 2.730 backbone; (2) recover nonane and the remaining octane with one easy final split; (3) abandon the unprofitable BBT naphthene train unless a clearly better cut emerges; (4) use remaining solves to tune the final split and trim costly columns. Step 1-2 now: R505's BBBB at boil-up 15 gives 99% octane overhead and leaves 106 mol/s bottoms containing about 62 nonane and 44 octane. A final 45-stage column with boil-up 8 should drive almost all octane overhead, yielding sellable nonane while recovering more octane. Prior BBT work failed: its C6 naphthene side products were only 84% and residual cuts were unsaleable, adding cost without revenue.

note: Trim the two easy heavy splitters: lower BBBB reflux and final polisher boil-up should cut cost and recover more octane while retaining saleable nonane.
notebook: PLAN: (1) Use R554's boil-up-6 polisher as the new baseline; (2) reduce wasted separation in the wide octane/nonane splits; (3) if purity holds, trim other costly columns while protecting the C5/C6 blend backbone. R554 at boil-up 6 gives 100% nonane and $92.7M/yr, versus 8 giving less nonane. The wide volatility gap suggests BBBB reflux 8 is excessive and final boil-up 4.5 may still exceed 95% nonane while recovering more octane overhead. BBT naphthene recovery and root double effect have both failed economically; avoid repeating them.

note: Combine my cheaper, higher-octane-recovery stripper with the proven strong polisher; its 90%-nonane feed should now yield saleable octane overhead and premium nonane bottoms.
notebook: PLAN: (1) Combine the high-octane-recovery BBBB 4/15 column with R601's strong nonane polisher; (2) trim the resulting heavy train if both products hold; (3) use remaining solves on the largest safe backbone savings. My BBBB 4/15 sends 229 mol/s of 99% octane overhead and a small 90%-nonane residue below, superior feed preparation to R601's 8/15. R601 shows 60/8/6 can make both polisher outlets saleable. Applying it to my richer nonane feed should recover about 62 mol/s nonane plus a little octane while retaining the cheap upstream stripper. BBT recovery and root double effect were uneconomic; avoid them.

note: Adopt the 3.219 plant and trim the easy cyclohexane/heptane finisher; its naphthene product has enough purity margin for fewer stages and lower reflux.
notebook: PLAN: (1) Adopt R649's profitable naphthene-plus-heavy train; (2) trim the easy cyclohexane/heptane finisher while retaining the 98%-blend product; (3) use remaining solves for safe backbone and heavy-train savings. R649 gains $155M naphthene revenue for $115M extra column cost and reaches 3.219. Its BBTB separates cyclohexane from heptane with a large 93%-cyclohexane overhead and 98% total naphthenes, so 45 stages and reflux 4 should preserve the blend while reducing both size and reflux cost. Avoid changing the difficult BBT feed-preparation cut until this is tested.

note: Restore the proven 3.219 plant and add a strong finisher to the heptane-rich cyclohexane column bottoms; recovering that residual heptane could add about $100M/yr net.
notebook: PLAN: Restore R649's 3.219 plant, then use the remaining solves to recover the valuable heptane-rich BBTBB residue; if successful, trim the new finisher or restore the best. R649's naphthene overhead is profitable, but its 118 mol/s bottoms still contain about 86 mol/s heptane worth roughly $135M/yr if sold. A second cyclohexane/heptane split with strong reflux and boil-up should reject nearly all cyclohexane overhead while retaining most heptane in a >=95% bottoms product. The 45/4 finisher was too weak (93% naphthenes), whereas 60/6 works, so do not weaken the upstream cut.

note: Adopt the proven milder cyclohexane/heptane finisher: it recovers more premium heptane at lower cost than my high-duty version, improving reward to 3.443.
notebook: PLAN: Adopt R743's proven 3.443 finisher, then use the final solves to trim that column while retaining pure heptane; restore the best if purity falls. My 60/8/10 finisher recovered only 55 mol/s heptane for $33.4M/yr. R743's milder 60/6/6 split recovers 62 mol/s, earns $14.1M/yr more product revenue, and costs $10.4M/yr less. The rest of the plant is identical, so this is a strict improvement and leaves scope to test 50/5/5 next.

note: Combine the proven premium-cyclohexane recovery with the cheaper upstream finisher, then trim the tiny binary splitter while targeting the 95% sale threshold.
notebook: PLAN: Adopt R791's proven 3.544 plant, combine its terminal cyclohexane recovery with R789's cheaper 45/5/5 heptane finisher, and test a matching trim of the tiny terminal binary splitter; retain the best valid result. R791 adds $55.2M premium cyclohexane for only $10.8M cost. R789 shows the upstream finisher retains 100% heptane at 45/5/5, saving $3.8M. The terminal feed remains essentially the same 57/43 cyclohexane/heptane binary, so 45/5/5 may preserve a saleable 95% tops while cutting cost; if not, restore the proven 60/6/6 terminal.

note: Adopt R838's best plant and make one final targeted strengthening of the tiny binary finisher: its heptane bottoms are already 93%, so modest extra reflux and boil-up may make both outlets saleable.
notebook: PLAN: Use the final solve on R838's proven 3.550 backbone and slightly strengthen its tiny cyclohexane/heptane binary finisher. R838 at 60/8/10 gives 100% premium cyclohexane overhead and 93% heptane bottoms, just below saleability. A 60/10/12 setting should retain the premium overhead while pushing the 26 mol/s bottoms over 95%, potentially adding about $47M/yr for only a small duty increase. All upstream settings remain exactly R838, so only the terminal column requires a new solve.
